stories.bridge: Every language you will forge in this course — Python, Java, C++ — descends from Hopper's heresy: write for humans, let the machine translate. Now let's build the backbone.

figures.name: Grace Hopper
figures.role: Computer scientist; rear admiral, US Navy; inventor of the first compiler

stories.hook: In 1952, Grace Hopper told a room of engineers that computers would one day understand English. They told her it was impossible.
stories.narrative: Hopper had a PhD in mathematics from Yale and had worked on the Harvard Mark I during the war, programming in raw machine code — the slow, error-prone ritual of translating human intention into binary by hand. By 1952 she was at Remington Rand, working on the UNIVAC, one of the first commercial computers, and she was struck by a simple observation: the translation work was mechanical, and mechanical work should be done by machines. Her proposal was radical: write a program that translates human-readable code into machine code automatically. She called it a compiler. Her colleagues were dismissive — the attitude, one later recalled, was 'it can't be done' — partly because early machines were so slow that the overhead seemed absurd, and partly because programming was considered a mathematical priesthood. Hopper had, in her famous phrase, a habit of moving ahead anyway. In 1952 she completed the A-0 system, the first compiler: it translated symbolic mathematical code into machine language, proving the concept. She then pushed further, arguing that the source language itself should read like English rather than mathematics — because the people with problems to solve weren't all mathematicians. That became FLOW-MATIC (1955–1959), the first English-like programming language, and it led directly to her role in the CODASYL committee that created COBOL in 1959 — a language designed so that managers and business analysts, not just scientists, could read programs. COBOL went on to run the world's banks, and much of it still does. The establishment never fully forgave her for being right too early, but every compiler, interpreter, and transpiler you will ever use is her idea, industrialized. She is also the source of the engineer's proverb you will need in this course: 'It's easier to ask forgiveness than it is to get permission.' The Navy, to its credit, eventually listened: Hopper rose to rear admiral, and the establishment that once dismissed her compiler ended up running on her languages. Her deeper vindication is structural — every layer of abstraction you will build in this course, from assemblers to type systems to the frameworks that compile beneath your notice, is the A-0 idea compounded. Write for humans; let the machine translate.
stories.title: The story behind the compiler
verifiedClaims: Hopper completed the A-0 compiler system in 1952
She participated in the CODASYL effort that produced COBOL in 1959

stories.bridge: Debugging is the oldest craft in computing — older, in a sense, than programming itself. Now let's learn the systems deeply enough to debug them properly.

figures.name: Grace Hopper
figures.role: Worked on the Harvard Mark II; popularized the 'bug' story

stories.hook: On September 9, 1947, at 3:45 in the afternoon, the Harvard Mark II stopped — because of a moth.
stories.narrative: The Harvard Mark II was an electromechanical giant — relays clicking, shafts turning — and that afternoon it simply stopped. The operators opened it up and found the culprit: a two-inch moth, trapped in relay number 70, its body bridging contacts that should never have met. Someone — the logbook doesn't say who — carefully taped the moth into the Harvard computation laboratory's log with the note: 'First actual case of bug being found.' Grace Hopper, who worked on the Mark II, loved to retell the story for the rest of her life, and it entered computing folklore as the origin of the term 'bug.' Here is the honest footnote, and it's worth more than the myth: engineers had been calling defects 'bugs' for decades. Thomas Edison used the word in an 1878 letter about his inventions, complaining about 'bugs' in his designs. Telephone engineers said it; radio engineers said it. What the moth gave the industry was not a word but a literalization — the perfect emblem for the moment every programmer knows: the machine is doing exactly what you told it to, and what you told it was wrong. The logbook page, moth and all, is preserved in the Smithsonian Institution, one of computing's founding relics. Hopper herself never claimed to have coined anything; she just knew a good story, and she knew that debugging — the patient, unglamorous hunt for the gap between intention and execution — would be the permanent condition of the craft. Every debugger, every core dump, every 3 AM stack trace in your future descends from that taped moth. The systems software in this module is where you'll learn to hunt: read the machine's state, form a hypothesis, and find your moth. There is a coda the folklore usually omits: the Mark II's operators logged the moth, removed it, and kept working — the first recorded incident response in computing history, complete with a ticket, a root cause, and a resolution. Your debugging in this module follows the same ritual, minus the tweezers.
stories.title: The story behind the first computer bug
verifiedClaims: The moth was found in Harvard Mark II relay 70 on September 9, 1947, and taped into the logbook
The logbook page is held by the Smithsonian
The term 'bug' for a defect predates computing; Edison used it in 1878

stories.bridge: A Christmas hobby project became the language of AI. Now let's learn it properly — from syntax to systems — and find out why the readable language won.
stories.hook: Over Christmas 1989, Guido van Rossum decided to build a hobby programming language to keep himself busy during the holidays.
stories.narrative: Van Rossum was a researcher at CWI, the Dutch national computing institute in Amsterdam, where he had worked on a teaching language called ABC — elegant, beautifully designed, but never widely adopted, partly because it couldn't reach the underlying system. During a quiet Christmas week in 1989, with the institute half-empty, he started writing a successor: a scripting language with ABC's readability but without its limitations, designed to glue together the CWI's Amoeba operating system work. He named it not for the snake but for Monty Python's Flying Circus — the British comedy troupe whose shows he was watching at the time, a naming joke that survived into the official tutorial's spam-and-eggs examples. The design bets were unfashionable in an era of C++ maximalism: significant whitespace instead of braces, dynamic typing, readability over cleverness, 'batteries included.' Python 1.0 arrived in January 1994; 2.0 in October 2000; the deliberate, painful break of 3.0 in December 2008. For years it was the friendly teaching language, the scripter's tool — while the 'serious' work happened elsewhere. Then two things happened: the data world discovered that readability scales to teams, and the machine-learning world discovered NumPy, which put C-speed arrays under Python's friendly syntax. By the 2010s the Christmas project had become the default language of AI research, data science, and automation — the backbone of this course's programming track. Van Rossum, who led the language as its 'Benevolent Dictator For Life' until stepping down in 2018, had won by insisting on the least fashionable virtue in programming: that code is read more than it is written. The language's governance became part of the story too: van Rossum's "Benevolent Dictator For Life" model held for nearly three decades until he stepped down in 2018, handing Python to a steering council. The community he seeded — the package index, the conferences, the culture of readability — is as much his creation as the syntax. You are joining that community in this course, not just learning its grammar.
stories.title: The story behind Python
verifiedClaims: Van Rossum began Python in December 1989 at CWI as a successor to ABC
The name honors Monty Python, not the snake
